planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall, setting the crown slightly below soil level to encourage new basal shoots. Ben Gairn was bred at Scotland's Scottish Crop Research Institute (released 1998, the predecessor institution later absorbed into the James Hutton Institute in 2011) specifically for improved resistance to blackcurrant reversion virus and its gall-mite vector, making it a lower-maintenance choice than older Ben-series cultivars in areas where that disease is common.

directions: Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade, and mulch well since black currants are shallow-rooted. Ben Gairn is a compact, Scottish-bred black currant valued for its tolerance of reversion virus and the big-bud mite that spreads it, in addition to the usual heavy, glossy-black fruit clusters typical of the Ben series. Renewal-prune one-third of the oldest wood each dormant season to keep the bush productive, since fruit forms mainly on one-year-old growth. Fruit is best processed into jams, syrups, or cassis rather than eaten fresh.

planting.note: Set dormant bare-root plants in early spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil; Risager is grown by specialty fruit nurseries as a productive black currant distinct from the common Ben-series lines.

directions: Risager grows into a vigorous, upright black currant bush bearing the intensely aromatic, tart fruit clusters typical of the species, best suited to jams, syrups, and cassis rather than fresh eating. Give it fertile, consistently moist soil and full sun to light shade, with a thick mulch layer to protect its shallow root system. Remove the oldest one-third of canes each dormant season, since black currants fruit most heavily on one-year-old wood.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Minaj Smyriou is carried by specialty berry nurseries as a distinct black currant selection.

directions: Minaj Smyriou produces the classic clustered, glossy black fruit of Ribes nigrum on a vigorous, upright bush. Grow it in full sun to light shade in moisture-retentive, fertile soil, mulching to keep its shallow roots cool and moist through summer. Prune out the oldest canes every winter to maintain a steady supply of productive one-year-old wood, and harvest once whole strigs have turned uniformly dark for the best balance of tartness and sweetness.

planting.note: Plant dormant stock in early spring or fall, setting the crown slightly below grade to promote new basal canes; Otelo is offered by specialty fruit nurseries alongside other European black currant selections.

directions: Otelo is a black currant cultivar grown for the same richly aromatic, tart clustered fruit prized across the Ribes nigrum group, used mainly for jams, cassis, and juice. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade and keep roots mulched and evenly moist, since black currants resent drying out. Renewal-prune a third of the oldest wood annually to maintain vigor and fruiting, as the heaviest crops form on one-year-old canes.

planting.note: Set dormant bare-root or container plants in early spring or fall into fertile, moisture-retentive soil; Blackdown is offered through specialty fruit nurseries as a black currant selection.

directions: Blackdown forms an upright, bushy black currant plant bearing clusters of the strongly flavored dark berries used for jams, syrups, and cassis. Grow it in full sun to light shade in fertile, well-drained soil with a steady moisture supply, mulching to protect the shallow root zone. Each winter, cut out the oldest third of the stems to keep the plant throwing vigorous new wood, which is where next year's heaviest fruiting will occur.

planting.note: Plant dormant stock in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Kantata 50 is sold through specialty berry nurseries as a distinct European black currant selection.

directions: Kantata 50 is a black currant selection producing the typically intense, tart fruit clusters of Ribes nigrum, used mainly for processing into jams, cassis, and juice. Site it in full sun to part shade in fertile, consistently moist soil, with mulch to keep the shallow root system cool. Remove the oldest canes each dormant season to maintain a renewing supply of one-year-old fruiting wood.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Kirovchanka is a cold-hardy black currant selection carried by specialty fruit nurseries.

directions: Kirovchanka produces the dense, glossy-black fruit clusters typical of hardy Eastern European black currant selections, prized for jams, syrups, and juice. Grow it in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to part shade, mulching well since the roots are shallow and dislike drying out. Prune out the oldest one-third of canes every winter to keep the bush productive on young wood.

planting.note: Set dormant stock in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Lentaj is marketed by specialty fruit nurseries as a notably sweet-fruited black currant selection.

directions: Lentaj is a black currant selection noted for milder, sweeter fruit than many European dessert-type cultivars, making it more palatable fresh in addition to its use in jams and syrups. Plant in full sun to part shade in fertile, consistently moist soil, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through summer heat. Cut out the oldest third of the canes each dormant season to keep the plant fruiting on vigorous young wood.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Hill's Kiev Select is sold by specialty fruit nurseries as a large-fruited Eastern European black currant selection.

directions: Hill's Kiev Select bears large, intensely flavored black currant fruit on a vigorous, upright bush, best used for jams, cassis, and juice. Grow it in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade, keeping the shallow roots mulched and evenly watered. Renewal-prune a third of the oldest canes out each dormant season, since the heaviest fruiting occurs on one-year-old wood.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container plants in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Tatran is a European-bred red currant offered by specialty fruit nurseries.

directions: Tatran bears long, dangling strigs of translucent red fruit typical of Ribes rubrum, tart enough for jellies and syrups but pleasant eaten fresh when fully ripe. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, since red currants tolerate more shade than black currants. Thin out crowded or aging stems each winter to keep air circulating through the bush and encourage new fruiting wood.

planting.note: Plant dormant stock in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Cascade is a red currant selection carried by specialty Pacific Northwest fruit nurseries.

directions: Cascade produces the clear, tangy red berries typical of Ribes rubrum on long strigs that make harvest quick once ripe. Grow in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade, mulching to keep the root zone cool and evenly moist. Prune out stems older than three years each dormant season, since red currants fruit best on younger wood and spurs near the base of older branches.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container stock in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Viking is a Northern European-type red currant offered by specialty fruit nurseries.

directions: Viking bears generous strigs of bright, translucent red currants with the characteristic sharp tang, useful fresh in small amounts and excellent for jelly, syrup, and baking. Site it in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, keeping moisture consistent through fruit set and ripening. Thin out old or crowded stems every winter to maintain good light penetration and steady annual cropping.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container plants in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Rosetta is a red currant selection offered by specialty fruit nurseries.

directions: Rosetta yields the long, dangling clusters of glossy red fruit typical of Ribes rubrum, tart and juicy enough for fresh eating when fully ripe but most often used in jellies, sauces, and syrups. Grow it in fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun to part shade, mulching to protect the shallow roots. Remove wood older than three years each dormant season to keep the bush cropping heavily near its base.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container stock in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; White Grape has received the RHS Award of Garden Merit as a whitecurrant and is widely offered by specialty fruit nurseries.

directions: White Grape is a whitecurrant selection of Ribes rubrum bearing translucent, pale-golden berries that are noticeably sweeter and milder than red currants, pleasant eaten straight off the strig as well as cooked. Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to part shade, since whitecurrants tolerate more shade than black currants while still cropping well. Thin out aging stems each winter to keep the bush open and productive.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container stock in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Zitavia is a whitecurrant selection offered by specialty fruit nurseries.

directions: Zitavia produces the pale, nearly translucent fruit typical of whitecurrants, with a milder, sweeter flavor than red currants that makes it a good choice for fresh eating as well as preserves. Grow it in fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun to part shade, mulching to keep the shallow root zone cool. Prune out the oldest stems each dormant season to maintain vigorous, well-lit fruiting wood.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained soil; Missouri Giant is a large-fruited golden/clove currant selection offered by specialty fruit nurseries and tolerates more heat and drought than European black currants.

directions: Missouri Giant is a selection of the clove or golden currant (Ribes odoratum) chosen for notably large, round berries that grow singly rather than in clusters and have a sweet flavor without the sharp, resinous aftertaste of European black currants. The shrub produces fragrant, clove-scented yellow spring flowers and reliable fall color in addition to fruit, making it a dual-purpose edible hedge plant. It tolerates heat, drought, and poorer soils better than Ribes nigrum cultivars, needing only light pruning of old wood each winter to stay productive.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Orus 8 is a black currant x gooseberry hybrid sold by specialty fruit nurseries, in the same vein as jostaberry selections.

directions: Orus 8 is a currant-gooseberry hybrid grown for large, dark, thin-skinned berries that combine gooseberry vigor with a milder, less tannic flavor than pure black currants. Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to part shade and mulch well, as with other Ribes hybrids the root system is shallow and resents drying out. Prune out the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the vigorous, thornless-to-near-thornless bush productive and easy to pick.
